questions.q: Why does an event's field list function as a 'public contract' once subscribers exist?
options: Because Salesforce legally requires a written API contract for every platform event
Because platform events cannot have more than five fields
Because changing a published event's fields can silently break subscribers you don't control and may not know about
Because only Salesforce support can edit platform event fields
questions.explain: Once a subscriber depends on an event's fields, changing them can break that subscriber without any warning, which is why event schemas deserve the same care as a public API.

questions.q: `Please_Cancel_Order__e` with an `OrderId__c` field is a design mistake because it violates which rule?
options: Events must always be high-volume
Fact, not command — this event instructs a subscriber what to do rather than announcing something that already happened
Events cannot carry an Id-typed field
Events must always be published after commit
questions.explain: A well-designed event announces a fact that already happened (Order_Cancelled__e), not a disguised instruction telling a subscriber what action to take.

questions.q: What is the safe way to handle a platform event field whose data type needs to change after subscribers are already live?
options: Change the field's type in place; existing subscribers will automatically adapt
Delete the old field immediately with no migration period
Data type changes are never a concern for platform events
Add a new field (or publish a new event version) and coordinate migration, rather than changing the existing field's type in place
questions.explain: Changing a field's type in place breaks subscribers expecting the old type. The safe pattern is adding a new field or a new event version and coordinating migration before removing the old one.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off between a 'thin' event and a 'fat' event?
options: Thin events are always high-volume and fat events are always standard-volume
Fat events cannot be subscribed to from Lightning Web Components
There is no real trade-off; fat events are strictly better in every case
Thin events keep the schema small but force subscribers into extra lookups; fat events save that lookup but grow the schema's surface area and contract-change risk
questions.explain: A thin event minimizes the schema but requires subscribers to look up extra detail themselves; a fat event avoids that lookup at the cost of a larger, harder-to-change schema.

questions.q: Per this lesson's field-design checklist, what should you check about data types before finalizing a new event's fields?
options: That every field is a picklist
That every field uses the Number type for consistency
That you're confident the chosen types won't need to change later, since revisiting a type is much costlier on an event than on a custom object
That no field is required
questions.explain: Because changing a published event field's type breaks live subscribers, the checklist calls for confidence in the chosen data types up front, since revisiting them later is far costlier than on an ordinary custom object field.
